chicken-drumstick-fried-coated-skin-coat.title: Chicken drumstick, fried, coated, skin/coating not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: A chicken drumstick that is deep‑fried in a crispy coating. The skin and coating are usually removed before eating. This item is a staple in fast‑food and quick‑serve restaurant menus.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken drumsticks are a popular fast‑food item because they are juicy and quick to prepare.
The coating often contains a blend of flour, spices, and breadcrumbs, giving it a golden crunch.
Deep‑frying is done at 175‑190 °C (350‑375 °F), creating a crisp crust while sealing in moisture.
In many regions the drumsticks are served with barbecue, honey‑mustard, or spicy chili sauces.
While chicken provides lean protein, frying adds extra fat content.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken drumsticks supply high‑quality animal protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: The meat provides niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: Chicken contains phosphorus, selenium and zinc, important for bone health and immune function.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: Protein and a modest amount of fat help keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Easily digestible
items.content: Chicken meat is generally easy on the digestive system, fitting most dietary patterns.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Deep‑frying adds significant saturated and trans fats, which can raise cholesterol levels.

items.title: Salt and additives
items.content: Coatings often contain salt and flavor enhancers, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to chicken proteins.

items.title: Frying by‑products
items.content: Overheating oil can produce acrylamide and other potentially harmful compounds.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Remove the coating and skin before consumption, leaving the tender meat. The drumstick can be split, dipped in sauce, or added to salads and sandwiches.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked drumsticks in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in a sealed bag at –18 °C (0 °F) where they remain good for about 2 months.

chicken-or-turkey-noodles-and-vegetables.title: Chicken or Turkey with Noodles and Vegetables in Cream, White or Mushroom Sauce

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of tender chicken or turkey meat, boiled noodles and a mix of vegetables (excluding carrots, broccoli and dark‑green leafy greens) served in a cream, white or mushroom sauce. The combination of protein, carbohydrates and vegetables makes it a balanced and satisfying meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken and turkey are lean sources of high‑quality protein that are easily digested.
Noodles made from wheat or eggs provide a quick source of energy.
Cream sauce is typically made from cream and flour, giving the dish a velvety texture.
Mushroom sauce offers a rich umami flavor and can be prepared with button or porcini mushrooms.
Excluding carrots, broccoli and dark‑green leafy vegetables makes the dish suitable for those with specific vegetable intolerances.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Poultry meat contains all essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Energy‑providing carbs
items.content: Noodles supply glucose that is rapidly converted into usable energy.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken and turkey are high in niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The meal provides iron, zinc and phosphorus, important for blood health and bones.

items.title: Benefits of mushrooms
items.content: Mushroom sauce adds beta‑glucans, which may support the immune system.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken or turkey.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Cream sauce can be high in saturated fats; people with high cholesterol should limit intake.

items.title: Monosodium glutamate
items.content: If the sauce uses prepared stock, it may contain MSG, which can cause headaches in sensitive people.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Sauces often contain salt; those with hypertension should monitor consumption.

content.title: How to Serve
content.content: Serve the dish hot, garnished with fresh herbs such as parsley and a sprinkle of grated Parmesan. A squeeze of lemon juice can brighten the flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days in an airtight container. When reheating, add a splash of water or broth to prevent the sauce from becoming too thick.

content.title: About
content.content: Pasta with cream sauce is a dish of cooked noodles tossed in a smooth sauce made from cream, butter, and often cheese. The creamy sauce gives the dish a velvety texture and rich flavor, while the variety of pasta shapes allows for many tasty combinations.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cream sauce originated in Italian cuisine in the 19th century as an alternative to tomato sauces.
Typical recipes use cream with a fat content of 20 %–35 % to achieve a thick consistency.
Any pasta shape can be used—spaghetti, fettuccine, penne—but broader noodles hold the sauce better.
The dish is traditionally finished with grated Parmesan or Pecorino, enhancing its aroma.
Variations may include mushrooms, spinach, salmon, or truffles in the sauce.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Pasta provides carbohydrates, a quick source of energy for the body.

items.title: Calcium from cream
items.content: Cream contains calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Durum wheat pasta supplies B1, B2, and niacin, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: When olive oil is added to the sauce, it contributes beneficial monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats.

items.title: Protein
items.content: Both pasta and cheese provide plant‑based and dairy protein needed for tissue repair.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Cream sauces are rich in saturated fats, so the dish should be eaten in moderation, especially by those with cardiovascular concerns.

items.title: Lactose
items.content: Cream and cheese may cause discomfort for people with lactose intolerance.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Traditional pasta contains gluten, making it unsuitable for individuals with celiac disease.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The meal is relatively calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight management.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Cream sauces often contain salt; those with hypertension should limit added salt.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook the pasta al dente, then toss it with hot cream sauce. Serve immediately, topped with grated cheese, freshly ground black pepper, and herbs. You can add sautéed vegetables, chicken, or seafood for extra variety.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry pasta in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Prepared sauce keeps in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Leftover pasta with sauce should be reheated gently on the stove, adding a splash of milk or cream to restore its creamy texture.

content.title: About
content.content: Pea salad with cheese is a light dish that combines boiled green peas, soft cottage or melt cheese, fresh vegetables, and a light dressing. It is popular as an appetizer, side dish, or a light meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Peas are one of the oldest legume crops, cultivated for over 7,000 years.
The cheese can be either fresh cottage cheese or aged cheese, changing the flavor and texture of the salad.
Pea salad is often served cold, but it can also be gently warmed.
In some regions, mint or dill is added for extra aroma.
The dish is easily adapted to a vegetarian diet by using a plant‑based cheese alternative.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Peas provide about 5 g of protein per 100 g, helping to maintain muscle mass.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Peas and cheese together supply B1, B6, and folate, important for metabolism.

items.title: Calcium and phosphorus
items.content: Cheese adds a substantial amount of calcium and phosphorus, supporting bone health.

items.title: Low fat when using low‑fat cheese
items.content: Choosing cottage cheese or low‑fat melt cheese can keep the calorie count modest.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy should replace cheese with a plant‑based alternative.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some melt cheeses can be high in salt; opt for low‑sodium varieties.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Legumes, including peas, may cause bloating in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled, garnished with fresh herbs. It can be added to sandwiches, used as a filling for wraps, or enjoyed as a standalone snack.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, keep cheese separate from peas to prevent excess moisture.

content.title: About
content.content: Fat‑free sour cream is a dairy product made from cream with almost all fat removed. It has a mild tangy flavor, a creamy texture, and a low calorie count, making it a popular substitute for regular sour cream in diet‑friendly cooking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Fat‑free sour cream contains about 0.5 % fat, whereas regular sour cream contains 20–30 %.
It is frequently used in sauces, soups, and desserts to add creaminess without extra calories.
Fermentation leaves probiotic cultures in the product, which can benefit gut health.
In the United States it is often labeled as “0 % fat sour cream” or “light sour cream.”
Sour cream can be made from cow’s or goat’s milk, with a slightly different taste profile.

items.title: Low‑calorie option
items.content: Fat‑free sour cream provides roughly 50 kcal per 100 g, allowing it to be used in weight‑management plans without adding many calories.

items.title: Good source of calcium
items.content: Calcium supports bone and teeth health; 100 g of the product supplies about 120 mg of calcium.

items.title: Contains probiotics
items.content: The fermentation process retains live bacterial cultures that may help maintain a healthy intestinal microbiome.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is essential for red blood cell formation and nervous system function.

items.title: Very low fat content
items.content: Minimal fat makes it suitable for people monitoring cholesterol intake.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Individuals with lactose intolerance may experience bloating, gas, or diarrhea after consuming sour cream.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein or whey proteins should avoid the product.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some brands add salt; those limiting sodium should check the label.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Fat‑free sour cream can be stirred into sauces, dressings, soups, casseroles, and desserts. It pairs well with berries, fruits, herbs, and spices. For a thicker consistency, whip it with a mixer.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the sour cream refrigerated at 0–4 °C in its original container. Once opened, use within 5–7 days. Discard if it develops an off‑smell, discoloration, or mold.

tuna-noodle-casserole-with-vegetables-an.title: Tuna Noodle Casserole with Vegetables and Mushroom Sauce

content.title: About
content.content: Tuna noodle casserole with vegetables and mushroom sauce is a baked dish that combines flaked tuna with pasta, a mix of vegetables (such as carrots, peas, broccoli) and a creamy mushroom sauce made from mushrooms and cream. The dish is popular in North America as a quick, comforting family dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Canned tuna is often used in casseroles because it is shelf‑stable and inexpensive.
The mushroom sauce adds a rich umami flavor and a silky texture.
In the United States the casserole is traditionally made with short pasta like elbow macaroni or shells.
Adding vegetables boosts the content of vitamins A, C and dietary fiber, making the meal more balanced.
The dish is frequently served in individual ceramic dishes, which makes reheating in a microwave convenient.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: Tuna provides a complete source of protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Tuna contains EPA and DHA, which support heart and brain health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The casserole supplies vitamin B12 and niacin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Fiber from vegetables
items.content: Vegetables add dietary fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Moderate saturated fat
items.content: When made with low‑fat milk or cream, the dish remains relatively low in saturated fat.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Tuna can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Sodium content in canned tuna
items.content: Canned tuna is often salted; choose low‑sodium varieties when possible.

items.title: Heavy metal exposure
items.content: Tuna may contain trace amounts of mercury; moderate consumption is advised, especially for children and pregnant women.

items.title: Lactose in the sauce
items.content: If the sauce is made with dairy, people with lactose intolerance should use alternatives.

items.title: Overcooked pasta
items.content: Over‑cooking the noodles can make them mushy and affect the casserole’s texture.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the casserole hot, usually in individual ramekins. Garnish with fresh herbs (parsley, dill) or a sprinkle of grated cheese. Leftovers reheat well in the oven or microwave.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cooked casserole in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑sized bags for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C before eating.
